stem: An inpatient Massachusetts hospice asks its pharmacy provider to keep a large non-patient-specific supply of acute-use controlled medications in the onsite ADD so the facility can avoid routine pharmacy deliveries. Which statement best describes the permitted acute-use purpose?
choices: The onsite supply is intended for timely palliation of non-life-threatening symptoms only until the pharmacy can fill and deliver the full prescription.
The circular defines a bridge-to-delivery supply.
The ADD may replace the pharmacy's routine dispensing service for any chronic medication.
The acute-use pathway is not routine bulk dispensing.
The facility may stock unlimited quantities if all products are Schedule VI.
Schedule VI also has category limits.
The stock is reserved only for life-threatening resuscitation emergencies.
The circular addresses timely palliative symptoms that are not life threatening.
The facility owns all ADD contents as soon as the machine is installed.
Contents remain pharmacy property until dispensed.
steps: Identify the inpatient hospice acute-use pathway
Apply its bridge-supply purpose
core: Hospice acute-use stock is a limited palliative bridge until the pharmacy can fill and deliver the full prescription.
facts: The pathway uses an onsite ADD for approved Schedule II-VI categories.
trap: Turning a bridge supply into routine floor stock.
distinct: New inpatient-hospice stock purpose; no current-bank equivalent.
anti_guess: All options describe plausible institutional-stock purposes.

stem: A pharmacy will place an acute-use ADD inside a Massachusetts inpatient hospice. Which requirements are part of the current hospice pathway? Select all that apply.
choices: Obtain a machine-specific Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration
The hospice circular requires a machine-specific CSR.
Determine whether a machine-specific DEA registration is required
The pharmacy must make that DEA determination.
Continuously monitor the ADD by video
Continuous video monitoring applies.
Transfer ownership of all cabinet contents to the hospice before any dose is dispensed
The pharmacy retains ownership until dispensing.
Skip prescription reconciliation because the medications are palliative
ADD dispensing must be reconciled with prescriptions.
steps: Identify hospice acute-use ADD storage
Apply registration, monitoring, ownership, and reconciliation rules
core: Hospice acute-use ADDs require machine-specific state registration, DEA assessment, continuous video, pharmacy ownership, and prescription reconciliation.
facts: General Massachusetts ADD requirements also apply.
trap: Assuming hospice status relaxes machine-level controls.
distinct: Hospice-specific ADD governance differs from Q0137 routine retail ADD use.
anti_guess: Each option is a realistic machine-control decision.

stem: A Massachusetts inpatient hospice has 18 licensed beds. What is the maximum number of Schedule II-V analgesic units permitted in its acute-use ADD under the current circular?
choices: 50 units
That analgesic cap applies below 10 beds.
60 units
That is a sedative/anticonvulsant value, not the analgesic cap for this tier.
75 units
That is a Schedule VI ancillary value for the largest tier.
100 units
11-20 beds permits 100 analgesic units.
150 units
That analgesic cap applies above 21 beds.
steps: Place 18 beds in the 11-20 tier
Apply the analgesic category maximum
core: An 11-20-bed hospice may stock up to 100 Schedule II-V analgesic units in the acute-use ADD.
facts: Sedative/anticonvulsant and Schedule VI ancillary categories have separate caps.
trap: Mixing category caps within the same bed tier.
distinct: New hospice-specific quantitative pathway.
anti_guess: Distractors are values actually used elsewhere in the official table.

stem: A community pharmacy receives by fax an otherwise valid Schedule II prescription for a routine ambulatory patient. The patient is not in an LTCF or hospice and the drug is not a qualifying narcotic compounded for direct parenteral or infusion use. May the fax itself serve as the original Schedule II prescription?
choices: Yes, every faxed Schedule II prescription is an original once a pharmacist receives it.
Federal law has limited fax-as-original exceptions.
Yes, if the prescriber calls afterward to confirm the fax.
A confirmation call does not create the stated exception.
No; absent a federal fax-as-original exception, the fax does not itself replace the required original prescription.
The ordinary fax is not the original.
No, because Schedule II prescriptions may never be transmitted by fax for any purpose.
Federal law has defined exceptions and other fax uses.
Yes, if the quantity is a seven-day supply or less.
Quantity alone is not a fax-as-original exception.
steps: Identify an ordinary Schedule II fax
Check whether any fax-as-original exception applies
core: A routine Schedule II fax does not serve as the original unless a specific federal exception applies.
facts: LTCF, hospice narcotic, and qualifying compounded narcotic prescriptions have separate exceptions.
trap: Treating fax transmission as equivalent to an electronic controlled-substance prescription.
distinct: Current bank covers emergency oral and EPCS pathways, not C-II fax exceptions.
anti_guess: Distractors invoke genuine adjacent rules such as confirmation and short supply.

stem: A pharmacy serving a long-term-care facility receives a faxed Schedule II prescription for an LTCF resident. The prescription is otherwise valid. Which federal rule is most relevant to whether the fax may serve as the original?
choices: The fax can serve as the original for the Schedule II prescription to the LTCF resident under the specific federal exception.
Federal law provides an LTCF fax-as-original exception.
The exception applies only if the Schedule II drug is a narcotic.
The LTCF exception is not limited to narcotics.
The fax is never an original because LTCF status affects only partial filling.
LTCF status also matters to this fax rule.
The fax becomes valid only after seven days have elapsed.
No such waiting period applies.
The facility must convert the prescription to Schedule III before the fax can be used.
A facility cannot reclassify the drug.
steps: Identify the patient as an LTCF resident
Apply the LTCF Schedule II fax exception
core: A faxed Schedule II prescription for an LTCF resident may serve as the original when federal requirements are met.
facts: The exception is broader than the hospice narcotic exception with respect to narcotic status.
trap: Importing the narcotic limitation from the hospice fax exception.
distinct: New setting exception rather than another C-II validity clock.
anti_guess: All answers use real C-II/LTCF concepts but only one identifies the correct fork.

stem: A hospice patient needs a Schedule II narcotic. The prescriber faxes a valid prescription to the pharmacy and clearly indicates on the prescription that the patient is a hospice patient. What is the federal consequence of those facts?
choices: The fax may serve as the original Schedule II prescription under the hospice narcotic exception.
The required hospice facts activate the exception.
The fax is an original only if the patient also resides in an LTCF.
Hospice is a separate exception.
Hospice status permits refills on the Schedule II prescription.
The fax exception does not create C-II refills.
The pharmacy must wait for a paper original before dispensing in every hospice case.
That would erase the federal exception.
The notation is irrelevant because hospice exceptions apply only to Schedule III-V drugs.
The exception specifically addresses C-II narcotics.
steps: Classify the drug as a Schedule II narcotic
Confirm hospice status is indicated
Apply the fax-as-original exception
core: A properly designated hospice Schedule II narcotic prescription may use the fax as the original under federal law.
facts: Hospice notation is material to this exception.
trap: Confusing a fax exception with refill authorization.
distinct: New hospice-narcotic fax fork.
anti_guess: Options deliberately mix hospice with other authentic controlled-substance concepts.

stem: A pharmacy receives a faxed Schedule II narcotic prescription that will be compounded for direct administration to the patient by continuous intravenous infusion. The prescription otherwise meets federal requirements. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The fax may serve as the original under the qualifying compounded-parenteral/infusion exception.
The described route and narcotic fit the exception.
The fax can never be the original because compounding makes the drug Schedule I.
Compounding does not reclassify it.
The exception applies only to oral compounded capsules.
The rule identifies qualifying parenteral/infusion routes.
The fax is valid only if the drug is nonnarcotic.
The exception is for a qualifying C-II narcotic.
A technician may choose a different route to make the fax exception apply.
The prescribed route and clinical order control.
steps: Classify the prescription as a Schedule II narcotic
Identify the compounded direct-infusion route
Apply the specific fax exception
core: Federal law permits the fax to serve as original for a qualifying Schedule II narcotic compounded for specified direct parenteral or infusion administration.
facts: The exception includes specified IV, IM, SC, and intraspinal uses under the regulation.
trap: Assuming every compounded C-II or every fax qualifies.
distinct: New formulation/route-driven legal fork.
anti_guess: The same controlled status is maintained across plausible route-based distractors.

stem: A practitioner wants to issue multiple separate Schedule II prescriptions for the same patient on one visit. Which federal conditions are consistent with the multiple-prescription pathway? Select all that apply.
choices: The prescriptions together may authorize up to a 90-day total supply
Federal law permits a total not exceeding 90 days when conditions are met.
The later prescriptions may include written instructions identifying the earliest date on which they may be filled
Earliest-fill instructions are part of the pathway.
The prescriptions must be issued for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice
Ordinary validity requirements still apply.
The practitioner should postdate each later prescription with its future fill date
The prescriptions are issued on the actual date; earliest-fill instructions are used instead.
The set automatically becomes refillable because it covers more than one month
Separate C-II prescriptions are not refills.
steps: Recognize separate C-II prescriptions rather than refills
Apply total-supply, fill-date, and legitimate-purpose conditions
Reject postdating
core: Multiple separate C-II prescriptions can cover up to 90 days when federal conditions are met; later fills use earliest-fill instructions rather than postdating.
facts: The regulation does not create a federal entitlement to receive 90 days in every case.
trap: Calling sequential prescriptions refills or postdating them.
distinct: Different practical decision from the bank's C-II no-refill items.
anti_guess: Each option tests a separate issuance condition rather than one obvious schedule fact.

stem: On August 14, a practitioner lawfully issues three separate Schedule II prescriptions intended for sequential fills. How should the later prescriptions be dated and controlled?
choices: Date each prescription with the future month in which the patient is expected to fill it.
That is postdating rather than using the actual issue date.
Use the actual August 14 issue date and place appropriate earliest-fill instructions on the later prescriptions.
That is the federal multiple-prescription structure.
Leave the issue date blank until the pharmacy receives each prescription.
A blank date is not the solution.
Convert the second and third prescriptions into refills on the first prescription.
C-II refills remain prohibited.
Have the pharmacy create new prescriptions when each month arrives.
The pharmacist does not create the practitioner's C-II prescriptions.
steps: Distinguish issue date from earliest fill date
Apply the multiple-prescription documentation rule
core: Later Schedule II prescriptions keep the actual issue date and use earliest-fill instructions rather than future issue dates.
facts: The total course must still satisfy the federal multiple-prescription conditions.
trap: Mistaking a 'do not fill until' instruction for permission to postdate.
distinct: Documentation fork within the 90-day pathway, not a refill question.
anti_guess: All options are plausible ways to stage monthly controlled medication.

stem: A Schedule II prescription is issued for a resident of a long-term-care facility and is being partially filled under the federal LTCF pathway. Assuming the prescription is not discontinued, how long may partial fillings continue from the issue date under this special rule?
choices: 72 hours
That clock belongs to a different C-II partial-fill situation.
7 days
That is an adjacent emergency-follow-up period.
30 days
That is not the federal LTCF/terminal partial-fill endpoint.
60 days
The special pathway permits partial filling for up to 60 days from issue.
6 months
That resembles a III/IV refill framework.
steps: Identify the LTCF special partial-fill pathway
Apply its 60-day endpoint
core: Schedule II prescriptions for LTCF residents or terminally ill patients may be partially filled under the special federal framework for up to 60 days from issue unless discontinued sooner.
facts: This is separate from stock-shortage and patient-requested partial-fill rules.
trap: Importing the familiar 72-hour remainder rule.
distinct: New C-II partial-fill exception, not Q0094 or Q0101.
anti_guess: Distractors are real clocks from neighboring controlled-substance rules.

stem: A pharmacy partially fills a Schedule II prescription repeatedly for a terminally ill patient under the federal special pathway. Which documentation principles apply? Select all that apply.
choices: Record the date of each partial filling
Each partial dispensing must be documented.
Record the quantity dispensed with each partial filling
Quantity accountability is required.
Document the patient as terminally ill for this special pathway
The special status must be indicated in the record/prescription framework.
Treat the remaining quantity as an ordinary refill transferable to another pharmacy without further analysis
A remainder is not an ordinary refill.
Continue partial fillings beyond 60 days solely because unused quantity remains
The special endpoint still applies.
steps: Identify terminally ill C-II partial filling
Apply per-dispensing records and special-status documentation
Apply the 60-day boundary
core: The special terminal/LTCF pathway requires traceable records for each partial and does not convert the remainder into an unlimited refill.
facts: The prescription may end earlier if discontinued.
trap: Focusing on quantity remaining while ignoring the special record and time limits.
distinct: Documentation layer separate from Q0160's deadline.
anti_guess: Three concrete record duties compete with two plausible remainder assumptions.

stem: A pharmacist receives a facially complete controlled-substance prescription but identifies unresolved facts strongly suggesting it may not have been issued for a legitimate medical purpose. The prescriber has a valid DEA registration. What is the pharmacist's federal responsibility?
choices: Dispense automatically because a valid DEA number transfers all responsibility to the prescriber.
Pharmacists share corresponding responsibility.
Resolve the red flags sufficiently before dispensing; if legitimate medical purpose cannot be established, do not knowingly fill an invalid prescription.
Corresponding responsibility requires an independent dispensing judgment.
Dispense first and investigate only if DEA later asks.
The duty applies before dispensing.
Change the drug and directions without prescriber involvement to make the prescription appear safer.
Unilateral rewriting does not resolve validity.
Ask a technician to assume legal responsibility for the final decision.
The pharmacist retains the professional duty.
steps: Separate facial completeness from substantive validity
Apply pharmacist corresponding responsibility to unresolved red flags
core: A valid prescriber registration does not remove the pharmacist's corresponding responsibility to ensure a controlled prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose.
facts: The duty is shared with the issuing practitioner.
trap: Treating DEA registration as a safe harbor for dispensing.
distinct: New substantive validity decision rather than required-elements review.
anti_guess: Distractors reflect real workflow temptations: defer, fill-then-check, or alter.

stem: A controlled prescription presents several unresolved diversion red flags. Which pharmacist actions are consistent with exercising federal corresponding responsibility before a dispensing decision? Select all that apply.
choices: Review the prescription and patient information for a legitimate medical-purpose explanation
Substantive review is part of the duty.
Contact the prescriber when appropriate to clarify material red flags
Verification can help resolve legitimacy concerns.
Document material verification information supporting the dispensing decision
Contemporaneous documentation supports accountable practice.
Ignore all red flags whenever the electronic prescription passes technical authentication
Technical authenticity does not establish legitimate medical purpose.
Dispense solely because another pharmacy previously filled a similar prescription
Another pharmacy's action does not discharge this pharmacist's duty.
steps: Identify unresolved legitimacy concerns
Use reasonable verification and documentation
Make an independent dispensing decision
core: Corresponding responsibility requires an independent, fact-sensitive effort to resolve material red flags before dispensing.
facts: Technical validity and medical-purpose validity are different questions.
trap: Letting EPCS authentication or another pharmacy substitute for professional judgment.
distinct: Process-oriented counterpart to Q0162's final decision.
anti_guess: Options are ordinary pharmacy workflow steps rather than extreme legal slogans.

stem: A community pharmacy receives an ordinary Schedule II prescription for methadone written solely for ongoing opioid-use-disorder maintenance. The prescriber is not using an applicable OTP dispensing pathway. Which federal principle controls?
choices: Treat it like any routine Schedule II pain prescription because indication never matters.
OUD indication changes the federal narcotic-treatment pathway.
Ordinary outpatient prescribing is not the regular federal methadone-maintenance pathway; OTP/narcotic-treatment rules must be satisfied.
Methadone OUD maintenance is specially regulated.
Convert methadone to Schedule III when used for OUD.
Indication does not reclassify methadone.
Fill it with five refills because OUD treatment is chronic.
Methadone remains Schedule II.
Dispense it as OTC medication if the patient has a prior OUD diagnosis.
Diagnosis does not create OTC status.
steps: Identify methadone and the OUD maintenance indication
Apply the federal narcotic-treatment pathway rather than ordinary C-II dispensing
core: Methadone's OUD maintenance indication invokes the federal OTP/narcotic-treatment framework rather than ordinary retail Schedule II prescribing.
facts: Methadone prescribed for pain follows a different controlled-prescription pathway.
trap: Using schedule alone while ignoring indication.
distinct: Q0015 tests methadone pain quantity; this tests OUD treatment authority.
anti_guess: The same Schedule II drug remains constant; indication drives the result.

stem: A practitioner who is not separately registered as a narcotic treatment program faces an emergency while arranging a patient referral for opioid-use-disorder treatment. Which statements describe the narrow federal emergency narcotic-dispensing pathway? Select all that apply.
choices: The practitioner may dispense, rather than prescribe, the narcotic medication under the emergency provision
The exception is framed as dispensing.
No more than one day's medication may be administered or given at one time
The emergency amount is limited per day.
The emergency treatment may continue for no more than three days while referral is arranged
The pathway has a three-day ceiling.
The three-day period may be renewed repeatedly whenever the patient has transportation problems
The emergency exception is not renewable/extendable that way.
The practitioner may write a 30-day retail prescription and label it a three-day emergency
That is not the dispense-only emergency pathway.
steps: Identify non-OTP emergency OUD treatment
Separate dispensing from prescribing
Apply daily and three-day limits
core: The narrow non-OTP emergency provision is a dispense-only bridge, one day's medication at a time, for no more than three days while referral is arranged.
facts: It does not create routine methadone maintenance prescribing authority.
trap: Confusing a three-day emergency dispensing exception with a three-day prescription.
distinct: Different from emergency oral Schedule II prescriptions in Q0023/Q0104.
anti_guess: Each option tests a separate feature of the emergency pathway.

stem: A practitioner appropriately treats opioid use disorder with a Schedule III narcotic medication that may lawfully be prescribed for maintenance or detoxification treatment. Which statement best distinguishes this from Schedule II methadone maintenance?
choices: Federal law can permit prescribing of qualifying Schedule III-V narcotic drugs for maintenance/detoxification when otherwise lawful, rather than applying methadone's ordinary Schedule II OTP restriction in the same way.
The schedule and treatment provision differ.
Every Schedule III narcotic becomes Schedule II when used for OUD.
Indication does not reclassify the drug.
Schedule III OUD medication can never be prescribed to an outpatient.
That overstates the restriction.
The drug becomes noncontrolled after the first OUD dose.
Treatment does not remove controlled status.
A pharmacist may independently prescribe any Schedule III OUD drug without separate authority.
The federal treatment rule does not create pharmacist prescriptive authority.
steps: Identify the drug as Schedule III-V narcotic treatment
Distinguish its federal OUD pathway from Schedule II methadone maintenance
core: Qualifying Schedule III-V narcotic OUD medications have a prescription pathway that differs materially from routine Schedule II methadone maintenance rules.
facts: State scope and all other prescribing requirements still apply.
trap: Applying methadone's Schedule II pathway to every OUD medication.
distinct: New schedule+indication interaction, separate from buprenorphine quantity questions.
anti_guess: All choices remain within OUD treatment rather than using obviously unrelated drugs.

stem: Which statements correctly describe Massachusetts practitioner registration for prescription controlled substances? Select all that apply.
choices: Approved activities involving Schedule II-V generally require both the Massachusetts MCSR and corresponding federal DEA registration
Both registrations are required for II-V activities.
A practitioner conducting approved activities only with Schedule VI may do so with the appropriate Massachusetts MCSR without a DEA registration
Schedule VI is state-controlled but not federally scheduled.
The DEA registration used for Schedule II-V activity must correspond to authorized schedules
The state and federal registrations must support the activity.
Massachusetts Schedule VI status automatically requires a federal DEA number
Schedule VI alone does not require DEA registration.
A DEA number by itself replaces the Massachusetts registration for Schedule II-V practice
Massachusetts also requires the MCSR.
steps: Separate Massachusetts Schedule VI from federal Schedules II-V
Apply state and federal registration requirements
core: Massachusetts practitioners need MCSR plus DEA authority for Schedules II-V, while Schedule VI-only approved activity requires the state MCSR but not a DEA registration.
facts: Massachusetts treats all prescription drugs as controlled substances within its own schedule system.
trap: Equating 'controlled substance' in Massachusetts with 'DEA-controlled.'
distinct: New prescriber-credential decision path, not prescription-element review.
anti_guess: Every option is a plausible state/federal registration relationship.

stem: A Massachusetts practitioner holds a valid professional license and an MCSR authorizing Schedule VI activity but does not yet have a DEA registration. The practitioner issues an otherwise valid prescription for an ordinary Schedule VI drug. Which registration statement is most accurate?
choices: The prescription is automatically invalid because every Massachusetts prescription drug requires a DEA number.
Schedule VI-only activity does not require DEA registration.
The practitioner may conduct the approved Schedule VI activity with the MCSR; DEA registration is required when moving into Schedules II-V.
That is the state/federal registration distinction.
The MCSR matters only for Schedule I substances.
The MCSR covers Massachusetts controlled-substance activity.
A pharmacy may assign its own DEA number to the prescriber.
A pharmacy cannot supply prescriber registration authority.
Schedule VI prescriptions are exempt from all Massachusetts registration requirements.
Schedule VI still requires appropriate MCSR authority.
steps: Identify the drug as Massachusetts Schedule VI only
Apply MCSR-only practitioner authority for Schedule VI
core: A properly authorized Massachusetts practitioner may conduct Schedule VI-only activity with the MCSR even before obtaining a DEA registration.
facts: Schedules II-V require both state and federal registrations.
trap: Assuming 'controlled' always means federally controlled.
distinct: Practical consequence of the credential distinction rather than Q0122's classification question.
anti_guess: Distractors reflect common DEA/MCSR misconceptions.

stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy prepares multi-drug single-dose compliance packages. Which statements reflect the current Board policy concerning Schedule II and III medications? Select all that apply.
choices: A qualifying Schedule II maintenance medication may be included under the current policy
The policy expansion includes S-II maintenance medication.
A qualifying Schedule III maintenance medication may be included under the current policy
The expansion also includes S-III maintenance medication.
Maintenance status is material; permission for some Schedule II/III maintenance drugs does not mean every acute Schedule II/III course belongs in the package
The policy is framed around maintenance medication.
Every Schedule II drug is categorically barred from a multi-drug single-dose package
That was superseded by the current maintenance-medication allowance.
Any controlled medication may be placed in the package merely because the patient requests convenience
Patient preference does not replace policy conditions.
steps: Identify the current Schedule II/III maintenance expansion
Separate maintenance therapy from acute use
core: Current Massachusetts policy allows Schedule II and III maintenance medications in multi-drug single-dose compliance packages, but does not create blanket permission for every controlled course.
facts: Other packaging, labeling, and dispensing requirements still apply.
trap: Remembering an older categorical prohibition or overgeneralizing the newer permission.
distinct: Compliance packaging is absent from the current question bank.
anti_guess: Correctness depends on maintenance status, not a single schedule keyword.

stem: Before a pharmacy deploys medications through a Massachusetts ADD, which actions support the required product integrity and inventory accountability? Select all that apply.
choices: Use manufacturer-sealed original packaging or compliant repackaging for a single dose/person
The policy preserves unit integrity.
Reconcile ADD inventory activity against what the pharmacy sent or expects to receive
Inventory reconciliation is required.
Track access and transaction activity so discrepancies can be investigated
ADD accountability includes access/event monitoring.
Combine unmatched loose tablets from multiple products to reduce cabinet space
That destroys product identification and accountability.
Delete access records after each shift once the cabinet count appears correct
The policy requires retained records rather than ephemeral logs.
steps: Apply package-integrity requirements
Apply transaction and reconciliation accountability
Reject convenience shortcuts that destroy traceability
core: A compliant ADD program preserves dose identity and maintains retrievable access, transaction, and reconciliation records.
facts: Medication losses remain subject to licensing-body reporting requirements.
trap: Treating automation as a reason to reduce traceability.
distinct: Capstone operational fork tying package presentation to accountability, not just Q0135 loss handling.
anti_guess: All options are concrete inventory practices a real pharmacy might encounter.
